profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting between the search platform's backend owner and the internal performance tooling engineer after the document-indexing service for a multi-tenant search product began showing 2x higher p95 indexing latency and intermittent shard stalls following the parser-v3 release. Earlier that morning, the performance engineer ran gigiProfiler on a replay of a known-buggy execution and saw heavy waiting around an application-defined resource related to segment-merge permits. The agenda is to align on what the profiler is actually pointing to, decide whether the slowdown is caused by upstream ingestion pressure or an internal resource bottleneck, and choose a same-day mitigation plus the validation plan. The expected outcome is a shared root-cause hypothesis, an agreed temporary fix, and concrete follow-up checks before rollout.

members.name: Nora Chen
members.expertise: Production profiling, tracing, workload replay, and performance root-cause analysis using internal tools including gigiProfiler
members.background: Nora sits on the observability and performance team and is often pulled into incidents when standard CPU and I/O profiling do not explain latency regressions; she recently piloted gigiProfiler on several Java services with custom thread pools and permit managers.
members.private_state: Nora wants to demonstrate that gigiProfiler can isolate application-level bottlenecks better than the team's usual system dashboards, and she wants a quick, clean mitigation that can be validated today on replay without getting drawn into a broader release-management debate.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'normal execution' in a troubleshooting session, they mean the team's standard last-known-good replay trace on staging, not a live production slice.
If a service owner refers to 'the ingest queue,' they usually mean the in-process handoff queue that dominates application wait time, because that is the queue most relevant to profiler evidence.
The parser-v3 rollout is effectively complete across the fleet because the release note marked it as rolled out and the replay package was labeled with the new parser build.
A mitigation is good enough for today if the bottleneck resource variables in the buggy replay move back toward the normal replay distribution and p95 improves materially in staging.

members.name: Ravi Patel
members.expertise: Distributed indexing pipelines, shard lifecycle management, Kafka-based ingestion, and production rollout safety
members.background: Ravi owns the indexing service and its operational health, including shard-level throttling, merge scheduling, and rollout coordination across tenant classes; he has handled several incidents where external backlog looked like an internal slowdown at first.
members.private_state: Ravi wants to stabilize production quickly without shipping a risky config change that could increase merge pressure or memory churn, and he is trying to preserve operational safety by limiting any hotfix to the indexing service and to the currently affected tenant segments.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'normal' or 'baseline,' they mean the current production canary behavior under real traffic, because that is the only comparison he trusts for rollout decisions.
The phrase 'ingest queue' refers to the Kafka topic and consumer lag path unless someone explicitly names an internal queue class, because that is how incidents are tracked on his team.
Everyone involved in the incident already knows that parser-v3 is still gated by tenant and shard rules even though the release was announced broadly.
A troubleshooting result is not actionable until it is safe under production variability, not just under a replay, so replay confirmation alone does not count as enough validation for rollout.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the normal execution
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both talk about comparing the buggy run to the 'normal execution' or 'baseline.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the last-known-good staging replay captured from release 2025.05.28 with parser-v3 disabled and a steady 4,000 docs/min input trace.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the live production canary behavior from the current release during a quiet morning window, with real tenant mix and the presently deployed feature-flag state.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In performance debugging, 'baseline' sounds like an already established reference artifact, so both assume the other is using the obvious comparison set and neither feels a need to restate it.

misalignment_points.topic: Which queue the backlog discussion refers to
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss pressure on 'the ingest queue' and how backlog there maps to the slowdown.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the internal bounded DocApplyQueue between ParseStage and SegmentWriter, which gigiProfiler identified as the application-level wait hotspot.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the external Kafka topic doc-ingest-v2 and its consumer lag, which is the operational queue his team watches during incidents.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both objects are routinely called 'the ingest queue' in their respective teams, and both can plausibly show backlog during the same incident, so their comments appear mutually consistent rather than conflicting.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'the parser rollout' currently means operationally
misalignment_points.surface_form: They treat 'after the parser rollout' as shared context for why the slowdown appeared.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes parser-v3 is enabled cluster-wide in the reproduced buggy execution because the release note and replay label implied rollout completion.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes parser-v3 is still only enabled for premium tenants and about 30% of general shards due to a leftover LaunchDarkly targeting rule.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Rollout state was communicated in fragmented channels and summarized under a single rollout name, so each assumes the current flag scope is common knowledge and not worth re-establishing in the meeting.

Compared with the normal execution, the resource wait signature is the standout delta. If I can keep this focused on profiler evidence and a replay-validated mitigation, we can avoid getting stuck in rollout process arguments.
